rv.q: As far-fetched as the plot gets, Neshat is a steadying force, infusing Sandra with a perfectly calibrated balance of anxious hope and effortless warmth — her smile alone is a masterpiece of complexity, in turn melancholy, joyous, triumphant, bittersweet.
As in that show, he is a whirling wonder here, in a skillful if sometimes overly dense adaptation he wrote alongside the production’s director, Michael Arden, and Susan Lyons.
Cale exquisitely spins this all out through realism, Hitchcockian twists and turns, Roman Polanski-style paranoia flourishes and red herrings, for a wildly entertaining theatrical ride.
Sandra is a diverting and unusual evening of theater, quiet but engrossing as it tells its meandering though complex tale.
Cale remains one of our most gifted storytellers
For a thriller, however, Sandra doesn't quite succeed as a thrill ride.
But he comes up short in this new piece, which feels overstuffed with plot and lacking in thematic resonance.
Sandra isn’t so much a character as she is a vacuum in her travels to Mexico to find a gay best friend who has disappeared there.
But despite a tireless performance by Marjan Neshat, Sandra feels more like Eat Pray Love dressed up as a half-baked thriller.
While not as engrossing as Cale's previous work, Sandra is a mostly entertaining, if not crackling, thriller.
How Sandra Jones becomes Sandra Rivers and how she ends up in coastal California is a story worth hearing.
When dream converges with reality, it makes for a very satisfying eipiphany.
A David Cale work is recognizable by its cinematic use of music to affect the mood of a scene.
The focal point keeps shifting, and as directed by Leigh Silverman (2ST's Grand Horizons ), too many unanswered questions are presented, and too many side roads are taken.

cn.t: Neshat impresses in this noir-tinged solo thriller, but critics find Cale's missing-person mystery more suited to another medium, with mediocre writing and a contrived plot that fails to generate theatrical suspense despite its intriguing premise.
